warmup.q: val fruit: Fruit = Apple("Gala", 180). What is the static type of fruit::class, the type the compiler gives it?
options: KClass<Apple>, because that's what the object really is
KClass<*>, because classes lose their type at run time
warmup.why: The compiler knows only that fruit is some Fruit; the real class shows up at run time. So it gives you "the class of some subtype of Fruit", which is KClass<out Fruit>, the same idea as Java's Class<? extends Fruit> from getClass(). Printing it at run time does show Apple. KClass<*> would throw away the useful upper bound, and KClass<Fruit> would promise more than the compiler knows.

opening:
In the last lesson, a second clerk stood at the storeroom door. Before each label was torn off, the clerk copied it onto a note: "apples". Today we pick up that note and look at it closely.

The shop's office keeps a card index, a small drawer of cards. Each card is filed under a note that names a tool, such as "Scale" or "Label printer", and says where to find it. Then the shop opens a second shelf. The apple shelf and the lemon shelf are both, in one word, "Shelf". The second card pushes the first one out, and nobody notices until someone fetches lemons for an apple order.

In code, the one-word note is a KClass. The trap is easy to fall into, because for plain classes a class behaves exactly like a type.

Type erasure and reified type parameters asked what can keep the whole type List<Apple>. In this lesson, we'll meet three objects that describe classes and types, ask a fruit for its class, cross over to Java's view, find what needs an extra library, and file the shelves under their whole labels. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the office card index, where the apple shelf and the lemon shelf fought over one card. A KClass is the one-word note: it names a class, checks values and casts, and on the JVM it's the same class as Java's Class. A value's note is a KClass<out T>. A KType from typeOf is the whole label, Shelf<Apple>, and Java gets one from a super type token.

Search your code for a map keyed by KClass<*> or Class<?>. If anything generic is ever stored in it, two of its entries may share one card.

Next, we'll meet types that must name their own kind. How can a setter in a base class return the subclass that called it?

sections.h: The one-word note and the whole label: KClass, Class and KType
sections.html:
Start with what a running program can ask. Lesson 3 of this track pulled classes and types apart. The class String backs two types, String and String?, and the class List backs List<String>, List<Int> and List<Apple>?. Lesson 8 added erasure: the compiler checks each type argument (the real type in the angle brackets, such as String in List<String>) and then drops it, so at run time each object keeps its class and nothing more. A box on the shelf still knows it's a box. It no longer knows what its label said.

Kotlin's reflection API, the part of the library that lets code inspect classes while the program runs, gives each idea its own object. Most confusion about KClass comes from mixing them up:

  • A KClass describes a class: String::class, Apple::class, List::class. It has no type arguments and is never nullable. This is the one-word note.
  • A Class is Java's object for the same class: String.class in Java, String::class.java in Kotlin. It's the same note, written on Java's paper.
  • A KType describes a full type: the class, its type arguments, and whether it may be null. typeOf<List<String>?>() gives you one. This is the whole label: "a list of strings, or nothing".
Java
Class<String> c = String.class;                                  // Java's class object
boolean same = new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass();   // true
// Java has no KType. The closest thing is a Type read from a declaration, such as a field:
Type t = Shop.class.getDeclaredField("varieties").getGenericType();   // java.util.List<java.lang.String>
Kotlin
val k: KClass<String> = String::class                 // Kotlin's class object
val c: Class<String> = String::class.java             // the Java one, for Java code
val t: KType = typeOf<List<String>?>()                 // List, with argument String, nullable
val same = ArrayList<String>()::class == ArrayList<Int>()::class   // true

To pick the right one, ask what you want to know. "What kind of thing is this?" is a question about a class, and a KClass or a Class answers it. "A list of what?" and "may it be null?" are questions about a type, and only a KType can answer them. In the figure, the arrows from the object at run time reach only the class objects. A KType comes from code: the compiler writes it down at a call site.

Here the clerk picture breaks a little. A real clerk could copy the full label onto every note. Kotlin writes a KType only where you ask for one with typeOf, and never stores it inside the object.

One warning before you run anything. Without the kotlin-reflect library on the classpath (the list of jars and folders a program loads its classes from), Kotlin prints these objects with a little apology attached:

class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available)
java.util.List<java.lang.String>? (Kotlin reflection is not available)

Nothing is broken. To print Kotlin names such as kotlin.String, toString() needs that library, so it falls back to Java names and says so. A Gradle project doesn't include kotlin-reflect unless you ask for it, while the kotlinc command-line compiler adds it by default, so the same code can print differently in the two. The fourth section of this lesson shows what else the library adds.

Objects know their class. Only code knows full types.

We've named the three objects. Next, we'll ask a piece of fruit for its own note, and see what type the compiler gives the answer.

What a KType knows that a KClass doesn't. println("classifier is List::class: ${t.classifier == List::class}, arguments: ${t.arguments.size}, nullable: ${t.isMarkedNullable}") }

Java has Class but no KType. The closest thing is * java.lang.reflect.Type, which you can read from a declaration (here, a field). */ public class ClassVsTypeDemoJava { static List<String> varieties = List.of("Gala"); // a declaration keeps its generic type public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Class<String> c = String.class; Type t = ClassVsTypeDemoJava.class.getDeclaredField("varieties").getGenericType(); System.out.println("Class: " + c); System.out.println("Type: " + t + " (read from the field declaration)"); System.out.println("ArrayList<String> and ArrayList<Integer> share a class: " + (new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass())); System.out.println("the field's Type keeps its argument: " + ((ParameterizedType) t).getActualTypeArguments()[0]); // Java types carry no nullability, so there is no twin of typeOf<String?>(). } }

sections.h: Asking a fruit what it is: x::class gives a KClass<out T>
sections.html:
There are two ways to get a KClass. A class literal, Apple::class, names a class you know while you write the code, and its type is exact: KClass<Apple>. A bound class reference, fruit::class, asks a value for its class while the program runs. Its type has an out in it:

Java
Fruit fruit = new Apple("Gala", 180);
Class<? extends Fruit> c = fruit.getClass();        // what getClass() is declared to return
Class<Fruit> strict = fruit.getClass();             // error: Class<CAP#1> cannot be converted to Class<Fruit>
Kotlin
val fruit: Fruit = Apple("Gala", 180)
val k: KClass<out Fruit> = fruit::class             // the class of SOME Fruit
val strict: KClass<Fruit> = fruit::class            // error: expected 'KClass<Fruit>', actual 'KClass<out Fruit>'

Why the out? The compiler knows only that fruit is some Fruit. When the program runs, it turns out to be an Apple, but it could have been a Lemon. So the most the compiler can promise is "the class of some subtype of Fruit". That is what out meant in lesson 4: the apple dispenser, which hands out some kind of fruit and takes nothing in. Java says the same with ? extends. Java's documentation for Object.getClass() says the result is Class<? extends |X|>, where |X| is the erased type of the expression.

The out doesn't stop you from using the answer. Everything that hands information out still works: fruit::class.simpleName, fruit::class == Apple::class, and cast, which hands back a Fruit. What you can't do is pass it where an exact KClass<Fruit> is required. The compiler makes no exception for final classes either: "Gala"::class is a KClass<out String>.

The other half of KClass<T : Any> is its bound, the "no nulls" sign from lesson 2. There is no class for a nullable type, because String? is backed by the class String. So KClass<String?> is an error, and so is asking a value that may be null for its class:

val kn: KClass<String?>? = null
Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'T (of interface KClass<T : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'.

val note: String? = ...
note::class
Expression in class literal has nullable type 'String?'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable.

Write note?.let { it::class } instead, and you get a KClass<out String>?, which is null when there's no value to ask. Java has no such check at compile time: note.getClass() throws NullPointerException when note is null.

A value can tell you only the class of some subtype. Use a class literal when you need an exact KClass<T>.

Kotlin's note and Java's note describe the same class. Next, we'll move between them, and put them to work.

sections.h: One note on two kinds of paper: converting, checking and casting
sections.html:
On the JVM, every KClass wraps a java.lang.Class, and two properties move you between them. You'll do it often at the edge of your code, where it calls a Java library:

Java
Class<Apple> c = Apple.class;
boolean isApple = c.isInstance(fruit);          // true
Apple gala = c.cast(fruit);                     // checked: ClassCastException if not
String name = c.getSimpleName();                // "Apple"
Class<?> runtime = fruit.getClass();            // the object's class
Kotlin
val k: KClass<Apple> = Apple::class
val c: Class<Apple> = k.java                    // KClass to Class, for Java code
val back: KClass<Apple> = c.kotlin              // Class to KClass
k.isInstance(fruit)                             // true
val gala: Apple = k.cast(fruit)                 // checked: ClassCastException if not
val lemon: Lemon? = Lemon::class.safeCast(fruit)   // null instead of throwing
k.simpleName                                    // "Apple"
fruit.javaClass                                 // the object's Class, like Java's getClass()

These are lesson 8's class-token tools, in Kotlin's spelling. isInstance is a checked is, cast is a checked as, and safeCast is a checked as?. (cast and safeCast are extension functions, functions added to KClass from outside it, in the package kotlin.reflect, so they need an import.) A failed cast throws ClassCastException: Value cannot be cast to workbench.generics.l09.demo.Lemon. Names work out of the box, simpleName and qualifiedName, and so does equality: fruit::class == Apple::class is true.

These checks are real, unlike the as T of lesson 8, because the KClass object exists while the program runs and knows what to compare against. The card index's get will rely on exactly that.

Two traps wait here. The first is from lesson 8: Int::class.java is the primitive class int, and Int::class.javaObjectType is java.lang.Integer, the boxed class whose objects wrap a number. The second is javaClass. On a value, fruit.javaClass is the object's Class. On a KClass, it would be the class of the KClass object itself, an internal Kotlin class. Kotlin 2.4.21 rejects it with a deprecation error that says what you meant:

k.javaClass
'val <T : Any> KClass<T>.javaClass: Class<KClass<T>>' is deprecated. Use 'java' property to get Java class corresponding to this Kotlin class ...

Which one should your code hold? Inside Kotlin code, prefer the KClass. It has safeCast, it's what other Kotlin APIs hand you, and it's what this lesson's card index files its cards under. At the edge, pass .java to the Java library and keep the KClass on your side.

Inside Kotlin, keep a KClass. Hand .java to Java code at the edge.

A note can name a class, check a value against it and cast. Can it also describe the class: its properties, its subclasses?

sections.h: The reference book in the other room: what needs kotlin-reflect
sections.html:
A KClass offers many more members: objectInstance, sealedSubclasses, isData, members, constructors, supertypes. Your code compiles against all of them, because the standard library declares them. But the code that answers them lives in a separate jar, kotlin-reflect, about 3.8 MB in 2.4.21. Think of it as a thick reference book about every class, kept in another room. A Gradle project doesn't fetch the book unless you add it, and without it these calls fail while the program runs:

Storeroom::class.objectInstance
KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError: Kotlin reflection implementation is not found at runtime. Make sure you have kotlin-reflect.jar in the classpath

Storeroom in the demo is a Kotlin object, a class with exactly one instance, and objectInstance asks for that instance. A rule of thumb holds up well: names, identity, instance checks, casts and typeOf are free; anything that lists or describes declarations needs kotlin-reflect. A declaration is a piece of code that introduces a name, such as a class, a property or a function.

Works with the standard library alone Needs kotlin-reflect
simpleName, qualifiedName, ==, .java, .kotlin objectInstance, sealedSubclasses, isData, isSealed
isInstance, cast, safeCast members, constructors, typeParameters, supertypes
typeOf<T>() with classifier, arguments, isMarkedNullable kotlin.reflect.full extensions such as createInstance()

The kotlin.reflect.full extensions fail differently, with NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/reflect/full/KClasses, because that class isn't in the standard library at all.

Java reflection needs no extra jar, and it works on Kotlin classes too:

Java
Apple.class.getDeclaredFields();                    // [grams, name]
Storeroom.class.getField("INSTANCE").get(null);     // a Kotlin object is a static INSTANCE field
Kotlin
Apple::class.java.declaredFields                    // the same Java reflection, from Kotlin
Storeroom::class.objectInstance                     // the Kotlin way: needs kotlin-reflect

So when a Java-level answer is enough (fields, methods, annotations), go through .java and skip the dependency. When you need Kotlin-level facts, such as whether a class is a data class, which subclasses a sealed interface has, or whether a property may be null, add kotlin-reflect, and add it on purpose.

Whatever you add, a KClass still has no room for "of apples". Back to the card index and its two shelves.

code.title: ReflectDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l09.demo import kotlin.reflect.full.createInstance import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** A Kotlin object: exactly one instance. The shop has one storeroom. */ object Storeroom { override fun toString() = "Storeroom" } class PaperBag { override fun toString() = "PaperBag()" } private fun attempt(label: String, block: () -> Any?) { val result = try { block().toString() } catch (e: Throwable) { // KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError is an Error "${e::class.java.simpleName}: ${e.message?.substringBefore(". ")}" } println("%-24s %s".format(label, result)) } /** * Run it twice: * ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ReflectDemoKt (without kotlin-reflect) * ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ReflectDemoKt -Preflect (with it) */ fun main() { println("-- standard library only") attempt("simpleName") { Fruit::class.simpleName } attempt("isInstance") { Apple::class.isInstance(Apple("Gala", 180)) } attempt("== and .java") { Apple::class.java == Apple("Gala", 180).javaClass } attempt("typeOf arguments") { typeOf<List<String>>().arguments.size } attempt("toString()") { String::class } println("-- needs kotlin-reflect") attempt("objectInstance") { Storeroom::class.objectInstance } attempt("sealedSubclasses") { Fruit::class.sealedSubclasses.map { it.simpleName } } attempt("isData") { Apple::class.isData } attempt("members") { Apple::class.members.map { it.name }.sorted() } attempt("createInstance()") { PaperBag::class.createInstance() } }

alt.title: ReflectDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l09.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Field; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.util.Arrays; /** * Java twin of ReflectDemo.kt. Java reflection needs no extra jar: it answers Java-level questions * (fields, methods) about Kotlin classes too. It doesn't know Kotlin ideas like data classes. */ public class ReflectDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("fields: " + Arrays.stream(Apple.class.getDeclaredFields()).map(Field::getName).sorted().toList()); System.out.println("methods: " + Arrays.stream(Apple.class.getDeclaredMethods()).map(Method::getName).sorted().toList()); // A Kotlin object is a class with a static INSTANCE field: Java's way to get objectInstance. System.out.println("Storeroom.INSTANCE: " + Storeroom.class.getField("INSTANCE").get(null).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("is it a data class? Java reflection can't say: it has no such idea."); } }

try.expect: Without the jar, the first five lines work (Fruit, true, true, 1, and class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available)). Then four lines show KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError: Kotlin reflection implementation is not found at runtime, and createInstance() shows NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/reflect/full/KClasses. With -Preflect: class kotlin.String, Storeroom, [Apple, Lemon], true, [component1, component2, copy, equals, grams, hashCode, name, toString] and PaperBag(). Java prints the fields [grams, name], the methods (with getters such as getGrams and the hidden copy$default), and Storeroom.INSTANCE: Storeroom. It has no notion of a data class.

sections.h: Filing the shelves under their whole labels: typeOf and super type tokens
sections.html:
Now the problem from the opening. A card index keyed by KClass works for the scale and the label printer, because neither has a type argument. It can't hold a Shelf<Apple> and a Shelf<Lemon> at the same time. Both have the class Shelf, so the second card silently replaces the first, and nothing fails until someone asks for apples and gets lemons. You can't even write the class of the type you mean:

val k = Shelf<Apple>::class
Only classes are allowed on the left-hand side of a class literal.

A KType keeps the type arguments and the nullability, and in Kotlin typeOf<T>() makes one. Java's answer is older, and cleverer than it looks:

Java
// A super type token. An anonymous subclass's superclass keeps its type arguments.
abstract class TypeRef<T> {
    final Type type;
    protected TypeRef() {
        type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0];
    }
}

Type t = new TypeRef<Map<String, List<Integer>>>() {}.type;   // java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>>
Kotlin
val t: KType = typeOf<Map<String, List<Int>>>()
t.classifier == Map::class                          // true
t.arguments.size                                    // 2: String and List<Int>
typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<Int>>()        // false
typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>?>()    // false: nullability counts

The Java version is the idea Neal Gafter named super type tokens. Lesson 8 said that erasure removes type arguments from objects but not from declarations, and a class's declared superclass is a declaration. So you create a throwaway anonymous subclass, a class with no name written right where it's used, new TypeRef<...>() {}, and read its superclass back with reflection. It's the label carved into a shelf's frame, where the clerk's hands never reach. The {} is the whole trick: two characters that do more work than any others in this lesson. Without them there's no subclass, and javac says TypeRef is abstract; cannot be instantiated. The trick has one well-known hole. Inside a generic method, new TypeRef<List<T>>() {} records the type variable itself, and prints java.util.List<T>.

typeOf has no such hole. Through a reified type parameter, one whose real type an inline function receives at each call site, it keeps everything: inline fun <reified T> tokenOf() = typeOf<T>(), called as tokenOf<List<String>>(), gives the full List<String>. That's the difference from lesson 8, where T::class kept only List. typeOf works without kotlin-reflect, apart from the apology in toString(), and KType equality is all a map key needs. File the shelves under typeOf<Shelf<Apple>>() and typeOf<Shelf<Lemon>>(), and the two cards sit side by side. That's the second half of the lab.

When a Java library wants a java.lang.reflect.Type, convert with typeOf<List<Apple>>().javaType, which in 2.4.21 still needs @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class). A super type token written in Kotlin works too, with a twist: it picks up Kotlin's declaration-site variance (the out and in written on a class) as Java wildcards. object : TypeRef<Map<String, List<Int>>>() {} prints java.util.Map<java.lang.String, ? extends java.util.List<? extends java.lang.Integer>>, because Map's V and List's E are declared out. javaType gives the plain form.

Key a container by KClass for plain types, and by KType for generic ones.

Know the limit, too. A KType exists only where the compiler wrote it, at a call site with a known or reified type. A box pulled off the shelf can still tell you only its class.

try.title: Capture a full type two ways
steps: Run TypeTokenDemo and TypeTokenDemoJava. Compare the two super type token: lines.
Find the line in the Java output where the token failed to capture the real type.
Uncomment the wrong move in each file. Predict, then run.

code.title: TypeTokenDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l09.demo import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType import java.lang.reflect.Type import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.javaType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** A super type token written in Kotlin: the anonymous subclass remembers its superclass's type argument. */ abstract class TypeRef<T> { val type: Type = (javaClass.genericSuperclass as ParameterizedType).actualTypeArguments[0] } /** typeOf through a reified T keeps the whole type. T::class here would keep only the class. */ inline fun <reified T> tokenOf(): KType = typeOf<T>() @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class) // KType.javaType still needs the opt-in in 2.4.21 fun main() { val t = typeOf<Map<String, List<Int>>>() // each variety's name, and the grams of each piece println("typeOf: $t") println("arguments: ${t.arguments.size}, second is ${t.arguments[1]}") println("javaType: ${t.javaType}") println("tokenOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>>(): ${tokenOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>>()}") println("List<String> == List<Int> as KTypes: ${typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<Int>>()}") println("super type token: ${object : TypeRef<Map<String, List<Int>>>() {}.type}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val k = List<String>::class }

alt.title: TypeTokenDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l09.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Java twin of TypeTokenDemo.kt: the super type token, the trick behind Jackson's TypeReference. */ public class TypeTokenDemoJava { static abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type; protected TypeRef() { // getClass() is the anonymous subclass; its generic superclass is TypeRef<the type you wrote> type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } } // the well-known hole: inside a generic method, the token captures the type VARIABLE static <T> Type listOf() { return new TypeRef<List<T>>() {}.type; } public static void main(String[] args) { Type t = new TypeRef<Map<String, List<Integer>>>() {}.type; // each variety's name, and the grams of each piece System.out.println("super type token: " + t); System.out.println("arguments: " + Arrays.toString(((ParameterizedType) t).getActualTypeArguments())); System.out.println("inside a generic method: " + TypeTokenDemoJava.<String>listOf()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Type k = new TypeRef<String>().type; } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints the typeOf result java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>> (Kotlin reflection is not available), arguments: 2, ..., the same type from javaType without the apology, true, false, and the Kotlin-written token java.util.Map<java.lang.String, ? extends java.util.List<? extends java.lang.Integer>>. Java prints its token as java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>>, its two arguments, and inside a generic method: java.util.List<T>: the hole. The wrong moves fail with Only classes are allowed on the left-hand side of a class literal. and TypeRef is abstract; cannot be instantiated.

aside.title: Why do JSON libraries ask for a TypeReference?
aside.html: JSON is a plain-text format for data, and a JSON library turns that text into objects. To build a List<Apple>, it must know the element type, and a Class can only say List, so it would fill the list with maps instead of apples. Java libraries therefore take a super type token: Jackson, a widely used JSON library, calls it TypeReference, and Gson calls it TypeToken. From Kotlin you can write object : TypeReference<List<Apple>>() {}, or pass typeOf<List<Apple>>().javaType where a library accepts a Type. Jackson's Kotlin module also reads Kotlin facts such as nullability, which is why it depends on kotlin-reflect.

compare.title: A type-safe card index in Java and Kotlin

java.title: CardIndex.java
java.html: import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; final class CardIndex { private final Map<Class<?>, Object> byClass = new HashMap<>(); private final Map<Type, Object> byType = new HashMap<>(); // Class<T> and T tied together: the compiler checks the pair <T> void register(Class<T> type, T impl) { byClass.put(type, impl); } <T> T get(Class<T> type) { Object impl = byClass.get(type); if (impl == null) throw new NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.getSimpleName()); return type.cast(impl); // checked } // generic tools: a super type token supplies the full type <T> void registerTyped(TypeRef<T> type, T impl) { byType.put(type.type, impl); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") // safe: only registerTyped puts values in <T> T getTyped(TypeRef<T> type) { return (T) byType.get(type.type); } } // index.register(Scale.class, scale); // index.registerTyped(new TypeRef<Shelf<Apple>>() {}, apples);

kotlin.title: CardIndex.kt
kotlin.html: class CardIndex { private val byClass = HashMap<KClass<*>, Any>() private val byType = HashMap<KType, Any>() // KClass<T> and T tied together: the compiler checks the pair fun <T : Any> register(type: KClass<T>, impl: T) { byClass[type] = impl } fun <T : Any> get(type: KClass<T>): T { val impl = byClass[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.simpleName) return type.cast(impl) // checked, no kotlin-reflect needed } inline fun <reified T : Any> get(): T = get(T::class) // generic tools: typeOf supplies the full type fun registerTyped(type: KType, impl: Any) { byType[type] = impl } fun getTyped(type: KType): Any = byType[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no card for $type") inline fun <reified T : Any> registerTyped(impl: T) = registerTyped(typeOf<T>(), impl) @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") // safe: only registerTyped<T> puts values in inline fun <reified T : Any> getTyped(): T = getTyped(typeOf<T>()) as T } // index.register(Scale::class, scale); index.get<Scale>() // index.registerTyped<Shelf<Apple>>(apples)

compare.note: Both are what Joshua Bloch calls a typesafe heterogeneous container (Effective Java, Item 33): one map holds values of many types, and the key carries the type, so get can return a T with a checked cast. The KClass half is a direct translation: KClass<T> for Class<T>, type.cast in both. The differences show at the call site and for generic types. Kotlin adds reified wrappers, so callers write get<Scale>() and registerTyped<Shelf<Apple>>(apples). For generic types Java needs a super type token object at each call (new TypeRef<Shelf<Apple>>() {}), while Kotlin's typeOf<T>() is computed from the reified T, with no subclass and no hole for type variables. In both, the full-type half needs one unchecked cast. It is safe because the map is private and filled only through the typed registerTyped.

worked.title: Build the card index's KClass half, then find where it stops

steps.say: A first draft files cards by class and hands back Any. It compiles, but every caller has to cast, and nothing stops a card being filed under the wrong note.
steps.code: class CardIndex { private val byClass = HashMap<KClass<*>, Any>() fun register(type: KClass<*>, impl: Any) { byClass[type] = impl } fun get(type: KClass<*>): Any? = byClass[type] } index.register(Scale::class, PlainLabels()) // compiles: a label printer filed as the scale val scale = index.get(Scale::class) as Scale // ClassCastException here

lab.title: A card index keyed by KClass, then by KType
steps: Skim Model.kt, which holds the fruit, two tools (a Scale and a LabelPrinter) and a generic Shelf<T>. Then skim Callers.kt, the same trick as lesson 8: the tests reach your inline functions through it. Run the tests: all seven fail.
Part 1. In CardIndex.kt, write register and get(type). Throw NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.simpleName) when no card is filed, and hand the tool back with type.cast(...).
Make the no-argument get() inline with reified T : Any, passing T::class on. Five tests should now pass, including the one that shows a KClass key holding only one shelf.
Part 2. Write registerTyped(type: KType, impl) and getTyped(type: KType) with the byType map. The missing-card message is "no card for " + type.
Make the two one-argument versions inline and reified, using typeOf<T>(). In getTyped<T>(), cast with as T under @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST"), and write one comment that says why the cast is safe.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: val impl = byClass[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.simpleName), then return type.cast(impl). cast needs import kotlin.reflect.cast.
typeOf needs import kotlin.reflect.typeOf. It works without kotlin-reflect, and two calls to typeOf<Shelf<Apple>>() give equal keys.
The reified functions must call only the public get(type), registerTyped(type, impl) and getTyped(type): a public inline function can't read the private maps.

drill.title: Write a KClass card index from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a card index with register(type, impl), get(type) and a reified get<T>() in Kotlin, using KClass keys and a checked cast. Then write the Java version with Class<T>. Finally, write the one line that gives you a key for List<String> in each language.

answer.html: class CardIndex { private val byClass = HashMap<KClass<*>, Any>() fun <T : Any> register(type: KClass<T>, impl: T) { byClass[type] = impl } fun <T : Any> get(type: KClass<T>): T = type.cast(byClass[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no card for ${type.simpleName}")) inline fun <reified T : Any> get(): T = get(T::class) } val key: KType = typeOf<List<String>>() // List<String>::class does not compile

alt.title: CardIndex.java
alt.html: final class CardIndex { private final Map<Class<?>, Object> byClass = new HashMap<>(); <T> void register(Class<T> type, T impl) { byClass.put(type, impl); } <T> T get(Class<T> type) { Object impl = byClass.get(type); if (impl == null) throw new NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.getSimpleName()); return type.cast(impl); } } // a key for List<String>: a super type token Type key = new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}.type;

recap: A KClass (or Java's Class) describes a class: no type arguments, never nullable. A KType describes a full type: the class, its arguments and its nullability. The one-word note and the whole label.
Apple::class is an exact KClass<Apple>. fruit::class is a KClass<out Fruit>, because the real class is some subtype; Java's getClass() returns Class<? extends Fruit> for the same reason.
Convert with .java and .kotlin; a value's Class is x.javaClass. isInstance, cast and safeCast are the checked is, as and as?.
Names, identity, checks, casts and typeOf work without kotlin-reflect. objectInstance, sealedSubclasses, isData, members and kotlin.reflect.full need it.
typeOf<Shelf<Apple>>() keeps type arguments, even through a reified T, and Java gets the same from a super type token. Key containers by KClass for plain types and by KType for generic ones.
The limit: a KType exists only where the compiler wrote it, at a call site with a known type. An object at run time still knows only its class.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "Why do we need typeOf at all? T::class already tells us the type." Explain the difference between a KClass and a KType in your own words, using the Shelf<Apple> and Shelf<Lemon> example, and say what Java uses instead.
explain.answer: A KClass describes a class, and every type built on that class shares it. Shelf<Apple> and Shelf<Lemon> are two different types, but both have the class Shelf, so T::class gives the same KClass for both, and a map keyed by it can hold only one of them: the second card replaces the first. Nullability is lost the same way, since String and String? share String::class. A KType describes the whole type: the class, its type arguments and whether it may be null. typeOf<Shelf<Apple>>() and typeOf<Shelf<Lemon>>() are different keys, so a card index keyed by KType can hold both. The JVM never stores this on objects, because of erasure; the compiler writes the KType down at the call site, which is why typeOf needs a known or reified type. Java has no KType. It uses a super type token: an anonymous subclass like new TypeRef<Shelf<Apple>>() {}, whose declared superclass keeps the type arguments and can be read back with reflection.

deeper.html:
Why doesn't a KType need kotlin-reflect, when so much else does? Because the compiler builds most of typeOf<T>(). At each call site it emits code that constructs the type from parts it already knows: the classifier (List::class), the arguments, the variance of each argument and the nullability flag. The standard library holds a small implementation of KType for that. Answering sealedSubclasses is different: it means reading Kotlin's own metadata out of the class file, and the reader for that metadata is what kotlin-reflect contains.

KType also records variance and stars. typeOf<MutableList<out Number>>().arguments.single().variance is OUT, and typeOf<List<*>>().arguments prints [*]. So a card index keyed by KType treats MutableList<out Number> and MutableList<Number> as different keys. That's correct, but it can surprise you: the key must be written with exactly the same type on both sides.

The docs page on reflection mentions that the kotlinc command-line compiler adds kotlin-reflect by default (you can opt out with -no-reflect). That's why a snippet that prints class kotlin.String in a quick command-line experiment prints class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available) inside your Gradle project. If you add kotlin-reflect to a program, add it on purpose: it's a 3.8 MB jar, and its first use loads and parses metadata, which costs a little time once per class.

Last, the javaClass rule from the third section has a reason. javaClass is an extension property on every type, and a KClass is a value like any other, so k.javaClass would mean the class that implements the KClass object, not the class it describes. The standard library declares a deprecated overload for exactly that receiver, and in 2.4.21 using it is an error. x.javaClass on ordinary values is unaffected.
